meta.analogy: The same bay: wheeled in and out for uvx, bolted to the floor for uv tool install.

seo.title: uv Python Tutorial #3 — uv tool install, PATH, and the Trap Everyone Hits (2026)
altTitles: uv tool install explained: shims, PATH and tool environments
seo.description: Chapter three of the uv course. When to keep a tool instead of borrowing it, what uv tool update-shell actually edits, where the shim lives, and why installing a tool does not let your project import it.
seo.breakdown: when to install a tool instead of borrowing one, how the PATH shim works, and why a tool is never an importable dependency.

scenes.narration: You installed the tool. Your terminal says command not found. Both are true.

Here's the whole thing happening. uv installs ruff, uv reports installed one executable, and then uv warns you in the very next breath that the folder holding ruff isn't on your PATH. Most package managers leave a beginner to work that out alone.

uvStage.headline: It warns you [immediately]
uvStage.premise: The install succeeded. The warning underneath is the part that matters.

steps.label: uv tool install ruff
out: warning: `~/.local/bin` is not on your PATH.
steps.detail: succeeded, and told you what is missing

scenes.narration: Welcome back. Last chapter you borrowed tools. This one is about the handful you use every day, and why keeping those is a different decision entirely.

data.title: Tools you actually keep
data.subtitle: uv, chapter three · install, PATH, and the trap

scenes.narration: So when should you borrow, and when should you keep? There's a simple test.

Borrowing is right when you reach for a tool now and then, because paying half a second occasionally costs nothing. Keeping is right when you type the name twenty times a day, because then you want the command itself, not a prefix in front of it.

uvStage.headline: Borrowed, and [gone] again
uvStage.premise: uvx wheels the tool in, runs it, wheels it out. Nothing stays behind.

steps.label: uvx ruff check .
steps.detail: perfect for the occasional tool

steps.label: ruff check .
steps.detail: and useless for the daily one

stage.label: nothing kept
stage.sub: you type uvx every single time

scenes.narration: uv tool install is the other mode. Same bay, but now the tool is bolted to the floor: uv builds it a permanent environment of its own, then puts one small file on your PATH that points at it. That one file is what makes the bare command work.

uvStage.headline: Bolted [down] instead
uvStage.premise: A permanent environment of its own, plus one small file on your PATH.

steps.label: uv tool install ruff
steps.detail: one environment, one shim

steps.label: ruff check .
steps.detail: no prefix. just the command.

stage.label: ruff on your PATH
stage.sub: one shim file, pointing at that environment

scenes.narration: You can see both halves. uv tool dir holds a whole environment per tool, complete with its own Python. The bin folder beside it holds nothing but the shims — one tiny file per command, and that's the only thing your shell ever sees.

uvStage.headline: Two folders, [two] jobs
uvStage.premise: One folder holds the environments. The other holds the shims on your PATH.

steps.label: ls "$(uv tool dir)"
steps.detail: a full environment, per tool

steps.label: ls "$(uv tool dir)/ruff"
steps.detail: its own Python, its own site-packages

steps.label: ls ~/.local/bin
steps.detail: and only the shim reaches your PATH

scenes.narration: Which brings us straight to the thing that trips everybody up on day one.

chapter.title: The PATH warning
chapter.subtitle: and how to make it stop

scenes.narration: The warning fires because the shim folder isn't in your shell's list yet. uv won't silently edit a shell profile behind your back, so the first install says so and waits for permission. One command fixes the list permanently, and a fresh terminal picks the change up.

uvStage.headline: One command, [then] restart
uvStage.premise: uv will edit your shell profile — but only when you ask it to.

steps.label: uv tool update-shell
steps.detail: it names the file it edited

steps.label: exec $SHELL && ruff --version
steps.detail: a fresh shell, and there it is

stage.label: ~/.local/bin
stage.sub: and now this one is on the list too

scenes.narration: On Windows a shim is a real executable file rather than a symbolic link, which is a Windows detail rather than a uv one. On macOS and Linux you get a link instead. Either way, one file per command, and removing that file is how a tool goes away.

uvStage.headline: A link, or a [small file]
uvStage.premise: Unix links to the environment; Windows copies a launcher. Same job either way.

steps.label: ls -l ~/.local/bin/ruff
steps.detail: macOS and Linux: a symbolic link

steps.label: dir %LOCALAPPDATA%\uv\bin
steps.detail: Windows: a real launcher executable

steps.label: rm ~/.local/bin/ruff && ruff --version
steps.detail: delete that one file and the tool is gone

scenes.narration: Now the misunderstanding. This one is worth stopping on, because almost everybody hits it.

chapter.title: The one big trap
chapter.subtitle: a tool is not a dependency

scenes.narration: You install ruff as a tool. Then you open a Python file in your project, type import ruff, and Python says no such module exists. Nothing is broken and nothing went wrong. Ruff lives in ruff's own environment, and your project is a completely different environment.

uvStage.headline: A tool is not a [dependency]
uvStage.premise: Two separate shelves. The tool sits on one, your project stands at the other.

steps.label: uv pip show ruff
out: warning: Package(s) not found for: ruff
steps.detail: not in your project. never was.

steps.label: uv run python -c "import ruff"
steps.detail: the command works. the import does not.

stage.label: wall
stage.sub: a tool you can run is not a package you can import

scenes.narration: So if your code needs to import a package, that package belongs in your project, and we'll do exactly that in a couple of chapters. Tools are for things you run. Dependencies are for things you import. Keeping those two ideas apart will save you an enormous amount of confusion.

uvStage.headline: Run it, or [import] it
uvStage.premise: The question is never which command. It is what you want to do with the thing.

steps.label: uv tool install ruff
steps.detail: because you want to RUN ruff

steps.label: uv add rich
steps.detail: because your code will IMPORT rich

scenes.narration: Finally, living with the tools you've kept.

Four commands cover everything. List shows what you've kept and what each one gave you. Upgrade takes one tool forward, or all of them at once. Uninstall removes a tool and its shim together. And uv tells you plainly when there's nothing to do.

uvStage.headline: Four commands, [that is all]
uvStage.premise: Everything you will ever do with an installed tool is one of these four.

steps.label: uv tool list
steps.detail: the tool, then the commands it gave you

steps.label: uv tool upgrade --all
steps.detail: plain english when there is nothing to do

steps.label: uv tool uninstall ruff
steps.detail: the environment and the shim, together

scenes.narration: One difference is worth watching for. When borrowing a tool, you pin the version with an at sign. When keeping one, you use the ordinary equals syntax instead. The mismatch catches people constantly, because the two commands otherwise look so alike.

uvStage.headline: The syntax [changes]
uvStage.premise: uvx pins with @. uv tool install pins the way pip always has.

steps.label: uvx ruff@0.3.0 --version
steps.detail: borrowing: the at sign

steps.label: uv tool install "ruff@0.3.0"
steps.detail: the at sign is not accepted here

steps.label: uv tool install "ruff==0.3.0"
steps.detail: keeping: the ordinary specifier

scenes.narration: And one rule straight from the documentation, worth repeating exactly: tool environments are not meant to be edited by hand. If a tool needs a plugin, reinstall the tool and name the plugin with dash dash with, so uv writes the plugin into a receipt file and remembers the pairing next time.

uvStage.headline: Do not [hand-edit] a tool env
uvStage.premise: Reinstall with --with instead, so uv records the extra and keeps it.

steps.label: uv tool install mkdocs --with mkdocs-material
steps.detail: the theme goes in the tool environment

steps.label: cat "$(uv tool dir)/mkdocs/uv-receipt.toml"
steps.detail: uv wrote it down, so upgrades keep it

steps.label: uv tool upgrade mkdocs
steps.detail: and the theme comes along automatically

scenes.narration: Here's a habit worth forming early. Pin the tools that decide whether your code is acceptable, because a linter that quietly upgrades overnight can fail a build nobody touched. Pin ruff, pin the formatter, and leave the harmless conveniences floating on latest.

uvStage.headline: Pin the ones that [judge] you
uvStage.premise: A linter that upgrades itself can fail a build where nothing actually changed.
uvStage.stageTitle: what to pin, and what not to

steps.label: uv tool install "ruff==0.16.4"
steps.detail: pinned, because ruff decides pass or fail

stage.label: a formatter
stage.sub: rewrites files, so surprises are costly

stage.label: httpie
stage.sub: a convenience, and nothing depends on it

stage.label: uv tool upgrade ruff
stage.sub: and upgrade deliberately, when you choose

scenes.narration: A kept tool also gets its own Python, which matters more than it sounds. Upgrade the Python you use for your own work and ruff carries on running against the interpreter ruff was installed with, because nothing in ruff's environment depends on yours.

uvStage.headline: Each tool gets [its own] Python
uvStage.premise: The interpreter inside a tool environment is not the one you work with.

steps.label: cat "$(uv tool dir)/ruff/pyvenv.cfg" | head -2
steps.detail: ruff runs on 3.13, whatever you use

steps.label: uv run python -V
steps.detail: and your own project is still on 3.10

scenes.narration: And because every tool has a private environment, two tools that need incompatible versions of the same library simply never meet. That's the chapter-zero problem solved once more, quietly, in a place you weren't thinking about.

uvStage.headline: Tools never [collide] either
uvStage.premise: One environment per tool, so two tools needing different libraries never meet.

steps.label: uv tool list
steps.detail: two tools, two private shelves

stage.label: wall
stage.sub: neither tool can reach the other shelf

scenes.narration: One more flag earns its keep. Adding dash dash isolated alongside dash dash refresh builds the environment from scratch and ignores everything cached, which is how you prove a failure is really the tool's fault rather than a stale copy sitting in your depot.

uvStage.headline: Prove it is not [stale]
uvStage.premise: A build from scratch, ignoring the depot, when the cached copy is the suspect.

steps.label: uvx --isolated --refresh ruff check .
steps.detail: a clean build, straight from the warehouse

stage.label: cache ignored
stage.sub: so a stale copy cannot be the explanation

scenes.narration: Quick check. You install ruff as a tool, then try to import ruff in your project code. What happens? Pause the video here and think it through properly first. Ready? It fails, because the tool lives in its own environment and your project is a different one.

quiz.question: Tool installed. Can your project import it?
quiz.why: Tools are for running. Dependencies are for importing.

scenes.narration: So, to recap. Borrow a tool you reach for occasionally, and keep the one you type all day. Installing a tool gives it a private environment and puts one shim on your PATH. And a tool you can run is never a package your code can import.

points.text: Borrow occasionally, keep the daily ones
Own environment, plus one shim on PATH
Run it with a tool. Import it with uv add.
